metadata.title: Two-Week Progress Review: 172 Videos, One Cadence
metadata.creator: Sanjana Rao
metadata.note: cli-explainer progress report for @HumanitariansAI, first-person Sanjana Rao (af_bella). SAME Claude intro/outro; dashboard-style data middle. Every number from the Video Reviews tracker, window Sep 6-19.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- SAME Claude UI as prior reels; first-person Sanjana
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Sanjana, a project manager at Humanitarians AI, and this is my two-week progress review -- a quick, honest look at the video reviews I ran over the past two weeks. I'll show you how many videos I reviewed, how many went up for the Professors to approve, how many needed changes, and the weekly rhythm I keep. Let's use AI to turn my tracker into a dashboard a stakeholder can read in a minute.

props.command: Turn my two-week video-review tracker into a clear stakeholder dashboard: how many reviewed, uploaded, and changed, and my weekly cadence.
output: 119 sent up for the Professors to approve
one week Mycroft, the next other projects

beats.role_note: the scale / why this matters to stakeholders; SHOW the volume
beats.narration_text: Here's the context. Every week, dozens of fellows across many projects submit videos, and someone has to review each one, give clear feedback, and decide what's ready for the Professors to see. That someone is me. Over these two weeks that meant one hundred seventy-two videos from thirty-eight fellows. At that volume, a gut feeling of 'it was a busy couple of weeks' isn't enough. Stakeholders need the actual numbers, and so do I.
beats.visual_intent: Animated counters climbing to 2 weeks / 38 fellows / 172 videos, with a grid of 38 fellow dots filling in, colored by project family. High volume made tangible.

beats.role_note: the system, shown BEFORE the numbers: cadence + per-video pipeline
beats.narration_text: Before the numbers, here's the system behind them, because the structure is the point. Two parts. First, a weekly cadence: I alternate every week -- one week I review the Mycroft project videos, the next week I review all the other projects. That keeps a huge queue from piling up on any single team. Second, every video runs the same pipeline: I review it, then it either goes up for the Professors to approve, or it goes back with specific changes, or it's blocked on a real issue -- and I check whether the code is on GitHub. Same path, every time.
beats.visual_intent: Top: a weekly-cadence toggle -- Wk1 OTHER PROJECTS <-> Wk2 MYCROFT, alternating. Bottom: a pipeline REVIEW -> {UPLOAD FOR APPROVAL / REQUEST CHANGES / BLOCK} -> GITHUB CHECK. Clean flow diagram, terracotta on the active path.

beats.role_note: ClaudeComposerAsk -- the analysis prompt; SPARK 'The ask,'
beats.narration_text: So let's build the dashboard with Claude. The ask is simple and specific: read my tracker, filter to the last two weeks, and give me the totals -- how many videos I reviewed, how many I sent up for approval, and how many needed changes. Specific in, checkable out.

props.command: claude "Read review_report tracker.xlsx (sheet 'September Videos'). Filter to 2026-09-06..2026-09-19. Print total videos reviewed, distinct fellows, and the sum of videos grouped by the 'Sent for Approval?' status."

beats.role_note: ClaudeCodeBeat -- the ACTUAL pandas; read the groupby that teaches
beats.narration_text: Here's what it wrote. It reads the tracker, keeps only the rows with a video count, and filters to my two-week window. Then two lines do the work: sum the videos, and group them by their approval status. That grouping is the whole report in one move -- it splits every video into uploaded, needs-changes, or blocked. And because this is real code reading my real sheet, every number you're about to see is one I can reproduce.

props.title: review_report.py
props.code:
# review_report.py  --  summarize my video-review tracker
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_excel("Humanitarians AI Video Reviews.xlsx",
                   sheet_name="September Videos")
df = df.dropna(subset=["Number of Videos reviewed"])
df["Date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Date"], errors="coerce")

# the last two weeks
last2 = df[df["Date"].between("2026-09-06", "2026-09-19")]

vids    = int(last2["Number of Videos reviewed"].sum())
fellows = last2["Person - ProjectName"].nunique()
status  = last2.groupby("Sent for Approval? ")["Number of Videos reviewed"].sum()

print("videos reviewed:", vids)      # -> 172
print("fellows:", fellows)           # -> 38
print(status)                        # Yes 119 | Needs Modifications 50 | No 3

beats.role_note: moving output -- KPI cards + status funnel; the headline numbers
beats.narration_text: Run it, and here's the headline. One hundred seventy-two videos reviewed. Of those, one hundred nineteen went straight up for the Professors to approve. Fifty came back with specific changes. And three were blocked on real issues. Watch the funnel: most of the work flowed through cleanly, and that fifty isn't waste -- it's the quality gate doing its job before anything reaches a Professor's desk.
beats.visual_intent: Top: four KPI stat cards -- 172 reviewed / 119 uploaded / 50 changes / 38 fellows. Below: a horizontal funnel from 172 splitting into 119 (green) / 50 (terracotta) / 3 (muted). Numbers large, no overlap, generous spacing.

beats.role_note: REVISION -- add the cadence breakdown; SPARK 'The revision,'
beats.narration_text: But a single total hides my rhythm, and the rhythm is what I actually want stakeholders to see. So let's revise the ask: split the same videos by week and by project, so the alternation shows up -- one week Mycroft, the next everything else. Let's see whether the data matches how I actually plan my weeks.

props.command: claude "Add a 'project' column (Mycroft vs Other) and a 'week' bucket (Wk1 Sep 6-8, Wk2 Sep 11-19). Group the videos by week and project and show me the split, with the peak review day in each week."

beats.role_note: revised code -- the map + groupby that reveals the cadence
beats.narration_text: The revision is just two ideas. First, tag each video as Mycroft or other. Second, tag it by week. Then group by both. That's it. The comments show what comes back: week one was other projects -- eighty-seven videos. Week two was Mycroft -- seventy-seven, with a few stragglers from other teams. The code found the exact cadence I keep, without me telling it the answer.

props.title: review_report.py | v2
props.code:
# review_report.py  --  v2: split by my weekly cadence
def project(name):
    return "Mycroft" if "mycroft" in str(name).lower() else "Other"

last2["project"] = last2["Person - ProjectName"].map(project)
# I alternate weeks: one week Mycroft, the next other projects
last2["week"] = last2["Date"].lt("2026-09-10").map(
    {True: "Week 1", False: "Week 2"})

by = last2.groupby(["week", "project"])["Number of Videos reviewed"].sum()
print(by)
# Week 1   Other     87    <- other-project week  (87 total)
# Week 2   Mycroft   77    <- Mycroft week        (85 total)
#          Other      8

beats.role_note: the better output -- cadence timeline (two peaks) + project donut
beats.narration_text: Re-run it, and there's the rhythm, week by week. Week one was the other projects -- eighty-seven videos. Week two was Mycroft -- eighty-five in total. Two weeks, two focused pushes, alternating exactly as planned. And across the whole fortnight the split is balanced -- ninety-five other-project videos and seventy-seven Mycroft. This is the picture I want a stakeholder to remember: steady, alternating, and nothing left to pile up.
beats.visual_intent: Left: two big week bars -- Week 1 = 87 (other projects) and Week 2 = 85 (Mycroft focus), labelled by focus, no calendar dates. Right: a donut -- Mycroft 77 vs Other 95 -- with a clean center total (172). Held side by side, no overlap.

beats.role_note: the stakeholder scorecard -- throughput, gate, cadence, GitHub gauge; honest caveat
beats.narration_text: So here's the two-week scorecard. Throughput: one hundred seventy-two videos reviewed. Quality gate: one hundred nineteen approved-path, fifty sent back for specific fixes -- the gate working, not rework wasted, and several fellows have already revised and re-uploaded. Cadence: alternating weeks, kept. And compliance: one hundred forty-six of the hundred seventy-two had their code on GitHub -- about eighty-five percent, with the rest already chased. One honest note: this counts videos reviewed, not hours, and 'changes requested' will keep turning into 'changes made' over the coming days.
beats.visual_intent: A compact scorecard: THROUGHPUT 172 | QUALITY GATE 119 / 50 | CADENCE alternating (Wk1 Other, Wk2 Mycroft) | a GitHub gauge filling to 85% (146/172). Footer honest-caveat line. Clean grid, high negative space.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- prompt READ ALOUD and discussed; greeting 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn -- and this one's for the PMs and stakeholders watching. If you keep a review or task tracker, you can get this same dashboard in one prompt. Paste your tracker into Claude and ask for the totals, the split by week and project, your GitHub-compliance rate, and three sentences you can drop straight into a stakeholder update. A good answer gives you the cadence and names the blocked items; a bad one just repeats your raw rows back to you.

props.segment: Turn your tracker into a dashboard
props.command:
Here is my team's review tracker for the last two weeks -- each row is a fellow's submission, with the number of videos, whether it was sent for approval or needs modifications, and whether the code is on GitHub.

[PASTE YOUR TRACKER / CSV]

2. Split it by week and by project so I can see my review cadence.
3. Flag the GitHub-compliance rate and anything still blocked.
4. Give me three sentences I can paste into a stakeholder update.
